title: Exploring K-12 Physical Education Teachers’ Perspectives on Opportunities and Challenges of AI Integration Through Ideation Workshops
venue: CHI Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems (CHI ’25)
extended_summary:
This paper examines how K-12 physical education (PE) teachers perceive the opportunities and challenges of integrating AI into their classes. The authors note that AI research in K-12 education has focused mostly on classroom-based STEM subjects, while PE remains underexplored despite its unique instructional and operational demands. Rather than testing a deployed AI system, the paper explores teachers’ lived challenges and their visions for how AI could support PE instruction and management.

The study used focus group ideation workshops with 17 in-service secondary school PE teachers in South Korea. Participants first discussed current classroom challenges, then received a short AI literacy introduction and generated ideas for how AI could support PE across four categories: perception, NLP, automation/optimization, and reasoning/prediction. They produced sketches, storyboards, and role-play scenarios, which were analyzed thematically. The context was in-service secondary PE teaching, so this is educator-centered and practice-oriented rather than student-outcome-focused.

The main findings show that teachers saw AI as potentially useful in four roles: operational assistant, personal trainer, group coach, and evaluator. These roles map to class management, personalized feedback, balanced team formation, and multidimensional assessment. At the same time, teachers raised concerns about institutional support, infrastructure, teacher technological readiness, alignment with PE goals, overreliance on AI, and student data privacy. The paper concludes that AI for PE should be designed as a supportive tool shaped by teacher needs, with strong attention to pedagogy, practicality, and ethics. This study is descriptive and exploratory, not causal, and it is not specifically about generative AI lesson-plan generation or lesson-plan feedback.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed qualitative HCI study using focus-group ideation workshops with 17 in-service teachers. It is descriptive and exploratory rather than causal, so it provides only one of the usual credibility criteria for intervention evidence.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper suggests potentially meaningful operational and institutional implications for AI in K-12 PE, but it does not test an intervention or report measurable learning gains. Its impact is therefore qualitative and unclear rather than demonstrably large or medium.

interventions.use_case: Participatory ideation workshops with in-service K-12 secondary physical education teachers to envision potential AI applications for classroom operations, personalized feedback, team formation, and assessment; not an evaluation of a deployed tutoring or feedback system.

finding.finding_summary: This is a descriptive qualitative study, not a causal evaluation. In a workshop with 17 in-service secondary PE teachers, participants repeatedly argued that AI could reduce teacher workload by helping with class operations, individualized feedback, team balancing, and assessment data management. No outcome effect sizes were reported because no AI system was implemented or tested.
finding.measure: Teacher perceptions and ideation themes from focus group workshops
finding.std_deviation: 0.37 (for pre-session AI attitude scale, not an outcome effect)

finding.finding_summary: Participants raised substantial implementation concerns alongside optimistic expectations, especially around institutional support, infrastructure, teacher tech proficiency, curriculum alignment, and student data privacy. The study reports qualitative themes rather than causal effects; no effect sizes are reported.
finding.measure: Teacher concerns and barriers discussed in focus groups
